why: B explains what 'grill Qn', 'plan review round n' and 'Dn' mean, which an outside reader needs for every citation that follows; A and C are equivalent terse variants and A's 'Choices the user made' reads a touch more naturally.

C separates the two complaints (SearXNG dependency, weak results) into labelled points so the reader sees the structure at once; B makes the SearXNG dependency explicit but in one paragraph; A assumes the reader already knows search depends on SearXNG.

C breaks the dense config and browser-choice material into one fact per bullet, names Consent-O-Matic as the owner of the v1.1.5 zip and spells out that 'rests' means not queried, while B compresses sentences until antecedents ('it ignores extensions', 'Its choices are reject') become ambiguous.

meaning_problems.B: 'since Chrome 137 it ignores extensions' and 'Its choices are "reject"' have unclear antecedents (branded Chrome / Consent-O-Matic), and the clipped 'None found: the search fails' and 'Only blocked earns the rest' make the reader reconstruct the condition.
meaning_problems.A: 'the pinned Chromium release zip (v1.1.5 today)' leaves it unclear that this is the Consent-O-Matic extension's release, not a Chromium build.

A and C state the review-then-fixed sequence in plain separate clauses; B's 'Thresholds Q1–Q3 as proposed are fixed' is awkward and its semicolon chain is harder to parse.
C makes explicit that query, papers and max_passages are parameters and writes 'There are no new tools' as a full sentence; B and A are the same text differing only by a comma.

A reads as one fluent sentence ('whatever the machine's locale or IP region'); C is equally complete but a little more stilted; B opens with the fragment 'English, fixed, for every engine' and separates the locale independence into a vague 'It doesn't depend'.
